changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For buyers whose pain is failed checkouts, stop leading with the average uplift. Lead with a diagnosis of why their own large orders get declined, in their words: 'the big baskets' and 'orders dying at the last step'. Follow it with a projected recovery figure built from their own decline export, for example: 'Here is why your big baskets fail at the last step, and here is what recovering them is worth in your numbers.'
changes.why: The average-uplift slide was shown, but by the time the offer reached the CFO it read as 'the same thing', while the specific explanation of big-basket declines is what landed with the champion.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: When the finance decider won't meet us, back the ROI claim with a one-page business case for the champion to hand the CFO. It should size the revenue lost to failed orders from the customer's own decline export and set it next to our price, so finance sees value against cost rather than rate against rate. Offer it as: 'A one-page business case in your numbers, that you can hand to finance.'
changes.why: The champion asked for 'a one-page business case' she could hand the CFO, but she got the deck and the pricing proposal, so the only page in the decision room was the controller's side-by-side rate comparison.

changes.change: Competitive response for when an incumbent bank cuts its rate in response to us: 'A better rate doesn't fix a single failed order.' Restate the cost of keeping the failures (their failure rate times the value of their largest orders) and pull the conversation back to declines instead of matching on rate.
changes.why: The bank countered with 'Just a better rate' and nothing else, and after that 'every email was the rate', so the conversation moved away from declines and we followed it.

changes.change: Opener for buyers whose pain is failed checkouts: start from their own measured failure rate, turned into lost revenue on their largest orders. Use the buyer's framing of wasted demand, along the lines of 'we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no', in place of acceptance or authorization-rate language.
changes.why: The champion arrived with her own failure rate ('Off their own dashboard'), concentrated on big baskets, and described the problem as wasted demand, which is sharper than our acceptance wording and was never turned into dollars.
